justice: Most of the corridor width is allocated to multiple motor-vehicle lanes, while no clear sidewalk is visible on either side of the road.
A narrow shoulder exists on the right, but it is bounded by a metal guardrail and does not provide an equivalent space for pedestrians compared with drivers.
No visible curb ramps, crosswalks, refuge islands, or tactile paving can be identified, limiting barrier-free access for many users.
The central landscaped median and roadside tree belt add visual value, but they do not compensate for the lack of dedicated space for non-motorized users.
safety: Lane markings are clear and the roadway is wide and straight, which supports predictable vehicle movement.
A metal guardrail separates the right edge from the roadside trees, reducing the risk of vehicles leaving the carriageway.
A truck is traveling close to the camera on the left and a two-wheeler is using the narrow right shoulder, indicating speed and size conflicts between different road users.
No visible pedestrian crossing, traffic-calming device, or protected cycling facility is present, so safety is mainly designed for through traffic rather than mixed users.
livability: The corridor appears to function as a high-speed arterial road with no visible shops, homes, or public destinations along the edge.
There are no benches, bus stops, shelters, plazas, or social spaces visible for daily street life.
Continuous trees and a landscaped median improve environmental quality somewhat, but the space remains primarily transport-oriented rather than people-oriented.
The absence of visible pedestrian activity suggests limited support for everyday community interaction.
sustainability: The rows of roadside trees and planted median contribute green cover and can help with air quality and heat mitigation.
Street lighting is present, which supports long-term public infrastructure use.
The very wide motor-vehicle roadway encourages car and truck movement more than low-carbon travel modes.
No dedicated bike lane, transit stop, or visible stormwater features such as bioswales or permeable paving can be identified.
aesthetics: The double rows of mature trees on both sides create a strong green visual frame.
The landscaped median with trimmed shrubs adds order and visual neatness to the road.
The pavement and lane markings appear well maintained, contributing to a clean appearance.
However, the scene is visually monotonous because it is dominated by long asphalt lanes, guardrails, and sparse roadside activity.
comfort: Roadside trees provide some shade at the edges, but the large exposed asphalt carriageway offers little thermal relief for users on the road itself.
No visible sidewalk, seating, or rest area is provided, reducing physical comfort for anyone not in a motor vehicle.
The wide open roadway and presence of a large truck suggest noise and stress for vulnerable users near traffic.
The road surface appears smooth and even, which benefits driving comfort and to some extent riding comfort for wheeled users.
walkability: No dedicated sidewalk is visible, making walking accommodation very poor.
The right edge is only a narrow shoulder next to a guardrail, which is not a comfortable or safe pedestrian path.
There are no visible crossings, curb extensions, pedestrian signals, or destination frontages to support walking trips.
The long uninterrupted roadway geometry prioritizes vehicle throughput over pedestrian connectivity.
bikeability: No protected bike lane or painted bicycle lane is visible anywhere on the corridor.
A two-wheeler is riding on the narrow right shoulder, indicating that non-car users must share marginal space beside fast traffic.
The wide straight roadway may offer directness, but the likely high vehicle speeds reduce cycling comfort and perceived safety.
No bicycle parking, intersection bicycle markings, or buffering elements for cyclists can be seen.
